name: Catalytic Spore Dispersal Drone CSDD-3 'Mulch'
description:
The CSDD-3 is a mid-altitude dispersal platform roughly the size of a cantaloupe, built around a pressurized bio-ceramic canister housing engineered fungal spore payloads. On deployment it rises to a pre-calculated ceiling, reads atmospheric thermals via onboard microbarometric sensors, and releases a calibrated spore cloud timed to drift across a designated kill zone at walking pace. Spores adhere to exposed skin and synthetic-organic hybrid tissue alike, triggering a rapid catalytic chain reaction in subcutaneous moisture that produces localized heat blistering and systemic inflammatory cascade over roughly ninety seconds.

What distinguishes the CSDD-3 from simple chemical drones is its terrain-reading persistence logic. If wind conditions shift before full dispersal, the drone repositions rather than releasing prematurely — operators in field trials noted it seemed to 'wait' for ideal conditions with uncomfortable patience. This behavioral loop, derived from IRONCLAD AGRISYSTEMS' commercial crop-dusting firmware, gives it an agricultural quality that many find more unsettling than outright aggression.

The canister is modular and field-swappable. Standard loadout is the Rot-3 spore blend, but the black market supplies Desiccant-7 (targeting mucous membranes) and Bleach-Null (suppressing biophotonic implant function). IRONCLAD officially denies any awareness of these aftermarket cartridges.
specifications:
dimensions: 18 cm diameter sphere, 22 cm with rotors extended
weight: 1.4 kg loaded
flight ceiling: 40 m operational, 120 m transit
payload capacity: Rot-3 spore canister, 180 mL pressurized
dispersal radius: 8–25 m depending on atmospheric conditions
onset time: 60–120 seconds post-contact
loiter time: 22 minutes at operational altitude
power source: Solid-state microcell, non-rechargeable field unit
guidance: Autonomous barometric + GPS dead reckoning
countermeasures: Sealed biosuite rated NBC-2 or higher
tactical_use: Operators typically deploy CSDD-3 ahead of forced entry operations to clear enclosed courtyards, rooftop positions, or bottleneck corridors. Because it loiters and waits for ideal dispersal conditions, teams can launch it during approach and trust it to act on arrival. Paired with acoustic or visual diversionary tools, it forces defenders to choose between holding position and taking exposure or breaking cover to avoid the cloud. Anti-vehicle use is limited but documented against unshielded driver compartments.
cultural_context: In GLMZ's mid-tier gang ecology, the CSDD-3 carries a specific class connotation — it's a 'rich crew's weapon,' associated with organizations that can afford to wait and plan rather than brawl. Carrying one signals patience and resources. Street-level operators call it 'the landlord's drone' partly as a slur, associating its slow, inevitable dispersal with eviction and debt collection. IRONCLAD AGRISYSTEMS' branding is still visible on most units, a faint crop-circle logo on the undercarriage, which has become darkly ironic shorthand in the Underbelly districts.
known_users: Corporate extraction teams (TESSERA CORPONATION security division)
Mid-tier gang enforcers with agricultural district connections
story_hooks: A series of unexplained skin-blistering incidents in the Terrace Market district traces back to a CSDD-3 unit that never received its shutdown command — it's still loitering somewhere in the ventilation superstructure above the market, waiting for ideal conditions.

An IRONCLAD AGRISYSTEMS whistleblower approaches the party with firmware logs proving the company's R&D division deliberately engineered the Rot-3 spore blend for human targets, not crop pests. The company has already sent a retrieval team.
A buyer wants five CSDD-3 units with Desiccant-7 cartridges for what they claim is a pest control contract. The address on the work order is a refugee resettlement block.
related_entities: Carrion Defense Works Autonomous Perimeter Defense Ecosystem

physical_description.visual_profile: A spherical biotech dispersal platform with an unsettling organic-mechanical hybrid aesthetic. The main body is a pressurized bio-ceramic sphere that resembles a scaled-up seed pod or fungal fruiting body. Four articulated carbon-fiber rotor arms extend from equatorial mounts, giving it a deliberate, patient stance even at rest. The overall impression is agricultural—something that belongs in a vertical farm—rather than explicitly hostile, which amplifies its menace.
physical_description.dimensions: 18 cm diameter (core sphere), 22 cm tip-to-tip with rotors extended. Rotor blades approximately 7 cm each.
physical_description.weight_description: Compact and moderately heavy for its size (1.4 kg loaded)—substantial enough to feel purposeful in a gloved hand, but small enough to fit in a tactical pack or be deployed from a shoulder-mounted launcher. Balance is centered, giving it a settled, almost patient quality.
physical_description.primary_material: Bio-ceramic pressure vessel (creamy ivory tone, slightly translucent at edges). Carbon-fiber composite rotor arms and mounting frame. Anodized aluminum sensor ring and motor housings. Sealed biosuite panel on lower hemisphere (brushed titanium inlay).
physical_description.finish: The bio-ceramic has a slightly matte, porous surface finish—like kiln-fired clay—with hairline micro-fracture patterns visible under close inspection. Rotor arms are satin carbon with micro-grip surface treatment. Sensor housings are brushed and micro-etched with calibration marks. The overall effect is utilitarian and field-worn, not polished.
physical_description.color_scheme: Primary: pale cream-to-tan bio-ceramic body. Secondary: gunmetal gray rotor arms and motor housings. Accent: faint bioluminescent cyan stripes around the upper sensor ring (passive status indicators). IRONCLAD Agrisystems branding in matte black block letters on equatorial band.
physical_description.grip_texture: Not typically handheld during operation, but if gripped (pre-deployment): the bio-ceramic surface is slightly warm and slightly tacky—deliberately textured to prevent dropping. Rotor guards are wrapped in thin rubberized EVA foam for transport. Deployment handle (if attached) is wrapped paracord-style in industrial-grade synthetic fiber.
distinctive_features: Pressurized canister seam running around the equator—slightly raised, with micro-venting ports for pressure equalization
Four rotor arms articulate independently, each with a small servo indicator LED (extinguished until armed)
Microbarometric sensor ring: a thin band of micro-holes circling the upper hemisphere, giving the appearance of a crown or fungal gills
Modular payload cartridge interface: a quarter-turn locking mechanism on the underside, with standardized IRONCLAD quick-disconnect coupling
Sealed biosuite panel: a small rectangular access port on the lower hemisphere, marked with NBC-2 certification stamps
Faint thermal scars and stress marks from repeated pressurization cycles—surface shows microscopic crazing consistent with field use
Silent vent passages: narrow slots that resemble natural seed pod fissures, designed to minimize acoustic signature
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: IRONCLAD AGRISYSTEMS logo (stylized wheat sheaf over an iron anvil) stamped in matte black on the equatorial band. Serial number etched in micro-font below. Model designation 'CSDD-3' in block letters. A small 'RESTRICTED — LICENSED USE ONLY' placard on the biosuite panel. Faint calibration marks and payload capacity stamps on the canister body, worn and partially obscured.
physical_description.condition_typical: Field-worn but meticulously maintained. The bio-ceramic surface shows minor stress crazing from repeated pressurization, but no significant damage. Rotor bearings are clean and responsive. There is a practiced restraint to its appearance—deliberately unremarkable, the kind of equipment that doesn't draw attention in a equipment manifest or surveillance footage. Occasionally carries drift dust or residual spore material in micro-fissures, cleaned before redeployment.
